Observed facts: 25‑year penetrating ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, controlled three years on infliximab; enterography 11 months ago showed no fistula. Recurrent right testicular pain and swelling yielded polymicrobial cultures (Peptoniphilus, Bacteroides, Citrobacter, Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella, Morganella). Surgical specimens demonstrated necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Acid‑fast, fungal studies and selected PCRs were negative; Bartonella PCR negative; Brucella testing not performed (no identified risk). Subsequent CT abdomen/pelvis showed no active bowel disease or fistula and the patient reported no gastrointestinal symptoms. At a later operation fresh cultures were not obtained; prior susceptibilities were reused. Prolonged antibiotics failed to resolve inflammation; infliximab was held.

Hypotheses: (1) Persistent polymicrobial infection from an occult enterovesical or enterogenital fistula not detected on CT. (2) Crohn’s‑related granulomatous orchitis/epididymitis, an extra‑intestinal manifestation, driving sterile inflammation despite negative cultures. (3) Unrecognised atypical infection (Brucella, Mycobacterium, Actinomyces) not covered by performed tests.

Proposed evidence to revisit before changing therapy: repeat high‑resolution pelvic MRI or contrast‑enhanced CT to exclude a hidden fistula; obtain fresh intra‑operative cultures and broad‑range 16S rRNA PCR; send tissue for Brucella serology/PCR, mycobacterial PCR, and Actinomyces culture; review histology for Crohn’s‑type non‑caseating granulomas versus infectious granulomas; assess infliximab trough level and anti‑drug antibodies. Decision on restarting or switching biologic should await these results.
